title: Learned initializer + Gauss-Newton/LM refinement in log-conductivity, MMSE readout: reach within ~1.5x of the Cramér–Rao floor
text: The parameter-to-observation map F: [0.5,2]^4 -> R^{4 x T} is smooth and locally well-conditioned (median Fisher condition number about 48). The noise is small (sigma=1e-3), so the likelihood is close to Gaussian around the truth. Under these conditions, a cheap learned initializer followed by bounded LM refinement through the exact forward model in log k should reach the local likelihood basin for nearly every sample. The importance-sampled posterior mean should then attain val rel_l2 < 0.03, compared with a CRB floor of about 0.0186. The posterior mean should also beat the MLE (mode) on k1 and k4, because their CR std (about 2%) makes box-prior shrinkage matter near the bounds. The objective is to minimise squared error, so the Bayes-optimal estimator is the posterior mean, not the MLE. The forward model is available and exact, since it is the same explicit FD scheme that generated the data, so there is no model-discrepancy term. The diagnostics put the information-theoretic floor at about 0.019, well below the 0.05 target. Purely data-driven regressors trained on 3000 samples must learn a 4-D nonlinear inverse map from a high-dimensional noisy time series, and they typically plateau above the CRB. Physics refinement removes that approximation error. Working in log k makes positivity automatic. It also roughly equalises sensitivity, because the diffusive time scale goes as 1/k, so d(log t_arrival)/d(log k) is approximately constant. That improves the conditioning of the Gauss-Newton normal equations. Ridge on log features is a near-linear inverse in the small-perturbation regime (a linearised Born-type map), so it should already land inside the basin. The context.forward used for refinement matches the data-generating simulator exactly: same grid, time steps, initial condition and sensor indices. The negative log-likelihood is effectively unimodal within a neighbourhood of radius about 10-20% in log k around the truth. Each sensor at indices 5, 15, 25, 35 sits inside a distinct segment, so each k_i has a dedicated, roughly separable sensitivity. The Laplace approximation is accurate enough that importance sampling on it gives a low-variance estimate of the posterior mean under the uniform box prior. The forward and Jacobian budget allows about 15 LM iterations x 750 val samples within the per-experiment limit.

The hypothesis is falsified if any of the following holds: (a) val rel_l2 >= 0.03; (b) per-parameter relative RMSE exceeds 2x the CR rel std for k2 or k3, which are the well-determined parameters, indicating optimisation failure rather than an information limit; or (c) the posterior_mean readout does not improve k1 and k4 RMSE over the mode readout, which can be checked by re-running with estimator='mode'.

Either the init lies outside the basin, which points to nonconvexity and argues for more extra_starts or a nonlinear initializer such as torch_mlp, or the forward model used for refinement differs from the generator. If the mode readout beats the posterior mean, the Laplace/importance-sampling scheme is degenerate near the box boundary, and MAP with a mild Tikhonov term is the better estimator.

author: researcher-mathematical
title: Global well-posedness test: initializer-free multistart MLE through the forward model achieves near-CRB accuracy (no learned surrogate needed)
text: With four segment-wise sensors and a centred pulse, the least-squares misfit J(log k) = ||F(k) - d||^2 has no spurious local minima over the prior box that attract LM from a small number of spread starts. Pure multistart MLE (3 starts, 30 iterations, log transform, no Tikhonov) should therefore reach val rel_l2 < 0.035. It should also be no more than about 15% worse than the hybrid of proposal 1, which would show that the learned initializer contributes speed, not accuracy. This separates two explanations for any hybrid success: a well-posed global landscape versus a learned initializer that is essential for escaping nonconvexity. The structural argument for a benign landscape is as follows. Heat travels outward from x=0.5, so the inner sensors (indices 15 and 25) are governed mainly by k2 and k3. k1 and k4 then enter through the outer sensors with an approximately triangular dependency. This suggests a sequential, near-monotone structure where larger k gives faster arrival and earlier decay, which favours a unique minimiser. If this holds, the method needs no training data at all and is immune to distribution shift. Its only remaining error is noise propagation, bounded below by the CRB of about 0.0186. If it fails, the failure itself localises the nonconvexity, for example k1/k4 trading off against k2/k3 through the shared flux at the segment interfaces. The multistart points are spread over the box (for example the prior centre plus randomised points), not all at the centre. 30 LM iterations are enough for convergence from any start in [0.5, 2]^4 when working in log space. There is no exact or near-exact non-identifiability across the whole prior. The harness Fisher diagnostic, a local quantity at 32 draws, is assumed representative. The forward model matches the generator, with no discretisation mismatch.

The global well-posedness hypothesis is falsified if either (a) val rel_l2 >= 0.035, or (b) more than 2% of samples end at misfit-inconsistent stationary points, which would indicate spurious minima. Comparing against proposal 1 tests the second claim: if the hybrid is more than 15% better, the learned initializer adds accuracy, not just speed.
data.if_fails: Misfit-inconsistent endpoints would show that J has spurious minima or long flat valleys, most likely along the k1/k4 directions. That would justify learned initialisation (proposal 1) or a continuation strategy, such as fitting early-time data first or estimating k2 and k3 before k1 and k4. If endpoints are misfit-consistent but rel_l2 is still high, the error is information-limited at those parameters (the local CRB is worse than the median), and only prior-informed MMSE estimators can help.

author: researcher-ml
title: Learned initializer + LM refinement with posterior-mean estimator approaches the CRB floor
text: A torch MLP trained on simulated train data gives a coarse estimate of k. A few bounded Levenberg-Marquardt iterations in log-k space through the exact forward model, followed by an importance-sampled posterior mean under the box prior, will reach val rel_l2 <= 0.03. That is within about 1.6x of the CRB floor of 0.0186 and well under the 0.05 success threshold. The forward model is cheap, available and exactly known: a 40-point explicit FD scheme with 200 steps. Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with known sigma, so the likelihood is exact. The Fisher condition number (median 48) is moderate, so the local problem is well posed once we start in the right basin. A learned map supplies that basin cheaply and amortized, and LM then removes the network's approximation bias. rel_l2 is a squared-error metric, which the MMSE estimator minimises in expectation. It also shrinks the poorly determined k1 and k4 (CR rel std about 0.02 and 0.018) sensibly near the box edges, where MLE clipping adds bias. The log transform respects positivity and makes the relative error scale roughly uniform. The harness forward model matches the data-generating simulator exactly: same grid, time steps, IC and sensor indices. Posterior is near-unimodal locally, so the Laplace approximation is an adequate importance proposal. The MLP initializer error (expected rel_l2 roughly 0.03 to 0.08) lies inside the LM basin of attraction. The per-sample LM cost for 750 val samples (and test) fits within the 120 s per-experiment limit with iters <= 15.

If both stall near 0.04 to 0.05, the CRB estimate at 32 draws underestimates the floor near the prior edges.

author: researcher-ml
title: Pure amortized inverse map with noise augmentation and log targets falls short of the success threshold
text: A purely data-driven MLP trained on 3000 simulated samples, with log-k targets, standardized raw sensor features and on-the-fly noise augmentation at the true sigma, will reach val rel_l2 in [0.035, 0.07]. It will beat the mean predictor (0.33) by more than 5x but will NOT match the forward-model hybrid. The gap will be concentrated in k1 and k4. The claim to be falsified is that the amortized map alone is already near-efficient at n=3000. The inverse map from about 800 noisy readings (4 sensors x about 200 times) to 4 parameters is smooth, but it must be learned from only 3000 points in a 4-D parameter space. Its achievable error is limited by approximation and estimation error, which is especially bad for k1 and k4, whose signals are weak (low SNR, CR std about 0.02). Noise augmentation matters because sigma=1e-3 is tiny relative to the signal: without it the network may fit noise-free structure and rely on directions that noise corrupts. This arm calibrates how much the forward model buys. It is also cheap at test time and serves as the data-driven reference against which proposal 1's improvement is measured. Training data are simulated with the same noise model as val. 3000 samples suffice to learn the map to a few percent in the well-determined segments k2 and k3. Standard scaling of raw features does not erase small but informative late-time signals; if it does, the log/sqrt features are an alternative.

author: researcher-experimental
title: Learned initializer + MMSE refinement beats both pure ML and pure MLE (competing-explanation control)
text: The dominant residual error of pure data-driven regression is approximation error of the inverse map (not noise), while the residual error of pure MLE comes from k1/k4 boundary-truncated, non-Gaussian posteriors. A hybrid that initialises LM with a torch MLP trained on noise-augmented simulated data, then reports the posterior mean under the box prior, will achieve val rel_l2 below both: specifically below 0.03 and at least 15% better than the best pure data-driven method. Two competing explanations for error: (A) learning-capacity/approximation limits from only 3000 training samples in a 4-D parameter space with ~800-dimensional features; (B) intrinsic posterior uncertainty for weakly determined end segments. The MLP alone should hit (A); LM refinement removes (A) and posterior_mean optimally handles (B) under rel_l2-like squared loss, since MMSE minimises expected squared error under the true uniform prior. Comparing this arm against a pure torch_mlp run and the pure MLE arm discriminates the explanations. Train/val inputs are generated with the same noise model; noise_aug with noise_scale matched to sigma regularises the MLP to the true input distribution. The MLP initialiser lands within the basin of attraction of the global minimum, so 1 extra start suffices. Laplace-based importance sampling of 128 draws is accurate enough for the posterior mean of a 4-D, near-Gaussian posterior. Squared-error MMSE is an appropriate surrogate for the rel_l2 metric (rel_l2 normalises by ||k||, roughly constant across prior).

title: Framing challenge: is the forward model even necessary? An amortized, noise-matched neural inverse with log targets
text: The inverse map from sensor time series to log k is smooth and low-dimensional, with 4 parameters and a well-conditioned Fisher information. A purely amortized estimator should therefore reach val rel_l2 <= 0.05 with no forward calls at test time. The estimator is an MLP trained on 3000 simulations, with log targets and noise augmentation matched to sigma = 0.001. Because it learns an approximation of E[k | data] directly, its gap to the physics posterior-mean arm should be at most 1.5x. If the gap is larger, the bottleneck is sample size, not representability. The task assumes that because a forward model is available, iterative inversion through it is the right tool. Amortized inference from the simulation-based-inference tradition makes a different claim. A regressor trained with squared loss on prior-drawn simulations estimates the posterior mean, which is the MMSE estimator, without needing a Laplace approximation. Log targets turn the roughly 1/k dependence of diffusion time scales into near-additive structure. Noise augmentation at the true sigma regularizes toward the correct likelihood smoothing. This arm tests whether data count (3000) or architecture is the limit. Comparing it with proposal 1 separates the cost of the estimator from the cost of approximation error. The training simulations are drawn from the same uniform prior as val and test, so squared loss yields an approximation of the posterior mean. The features are on comparable scales after standard scaling, and no sensor channel is dominated by near-zero readings late in time. 3000 samples are enough to cover a 4-D box at the resolution required for about 2% error, given a smooth map. Early stopping on an internal split does not touch the test data.

text: rel_l2 is a squared-error risk, so the Bayes-optimal estimator is the posterior mean under the uniform box prior, not the MLE or the mode. Near the bounds 0.5 and 2.0, the likelihood is asymmetrically clipped by the prior, so the mode is biased toward the boundary while the posterior mean is pulled inward. Working in log k makes the Laplace approximation more Gaussian, because diffusion time scales roughly like 1/k. The learned initializer removes the multistart cost and the risk of local minima. A Fisher condition number of about 48 suggests that LM converges in a few iterations from a good start. The forward model passed through context matches the simulator that generated the data, with the same explicit FD scheme, 40 points and 200 steps. The noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma = 0.001, so the Gauss-Newton Laplace approximation is reasonable in log-k space. An extra_trees initializer lands inside the basin of attraction of the global minimum for most samples. The forward and Jacobian evaluations for 750 val samples at about 10 iterations fit inside the 120 s per-experiment limit.
